intro: One cello supplies both a moving surface and an implied bass. This complete Prelude opens the six-movement suite; the remaining dances are not included in this recording.
question: How can a single line make a bass and harmony remain audible?

sections.label: Broken-chord opening
sections.mNote: repeated note patterns outline changing harmony

sections.label: Freer figuration over the dominant
sections.mNote: scale figures and repeated notes extend the route home

sections.label: Closing build and G-major cadence
sections.mNote: rising figures lead into the final tonic chord

cues.title: A chord unfolded in time
cues.text: The opening takes the notes of a G-major chord one after another rather than striking them together. Low notes keep a bass in the ear while the bow moves through higher notes: one cello implies several layers without an accompanist.
cues.evidence: The score’s first bar outlines G, D and B in continuous semiquavers. The analysis identifies G-major material in the opening windows; no particular bow stroke is timed.

cues.title: Follow the lowest notes
cues.text: Across the broken-chord writing, follow the low note at the beginning of a figure. The upper pattern can remain recognisable while that bass changes the harmony, making movement through keys audible without a separate bass instrument.
cues.evidence: The opening score changes bass and harmony within recurring semiquaver shapes. This instruction concerns the texture generally, not a claim about a particular chord at 0:30.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A copy leaves choices
cues.text: Anna Magdalena Bach’s manuscript copy is a central source for the cello suites. Its slurs leave performers difficult choices about grouping the notes; a surviving written line does not remove the need for decisions about the bow.
cues.evidence: Netherlands Bach Society, BWV 1007, discusses Anna Magdalena’s manuscript and its ambiguous slurs: https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-1007. The note does not claim this recording follows that manuscript’s bowings.

cues.title: The pattern becomes freer
cues.text: In the latter part of the Prelude, scales and changing figures loosen the opening’s regular broken-chord pattern. D, the dominant of G, remains a source of tension: busy surface movement can delay the eventual return home.
cues.evidence: The 42-bar score changes from regular arpeggiation to freer figuration around the fermata in bar 22. Boundaries at 0:56, 1:00 and 1:04 surround the proportional midpoint; D-centred material persists in the report. The 1:04 section point is approximate, not a located fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A court-period collection
cues.text: The suites are generally dated to Bach’s Köthen years, 1717–23. The Prelude precedes an Allemande, Courante, Sarabande, paired Minuets and Gigue: it prepares a sequence of dances rather than standing as the entire suite.
cues.evidence: Netherlands Bach Society BWV 1007 gives the broad date range and six-movement order; the exact composition date is not established. Bach-Archiv Leipzig documents the Köthen appointment in 1717.

cues.title: Building towards the tonic
cues.text: The closing stretch presses upward before settling in G major. Listen for repeated notes acting as a fixed point underneath the changing upper line; the final chord makes explicit the harmony that the earlier single notes could only imply.
cues.evidence: Score bars 37–41 build towards the final G-major chord in bar 42. The report’s strongest boundaries are 1:46 and 1:54, with high relative level through 1:50–2:00 and a final G-major region. No individual chromatic pitch is timestamped.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bow leaves resonance
cues.text: After the closing chord, the recorded sound decays rapidly. Compare that sustained ending with the separate attacks of the opening: the final harmony can remain in the ear after the motion has stopped.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −11.5 dB at 2:00 to −41.3 dB at 2:05 and −71.5 dB at 2:10. This identifies the decay, not the exact final bow release.

transitions.title: An arpeggio opens into a freer line
transitions.how: The regular opening figuration reaches a written pause on D and then releases a more freely moving line. Scales and changing note groupings replace the repeated arpeggio shape, but the dominant region keeps G major waiting. The contrast comes from the organisation of a single cello part, not a new instrument or a new movement: the line can suggest an improvised continuation while the harmonic goal remains controlled.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia 517, Schirmer 1916 source, Prelude bar 22 contains the fermata and subsequent running line. The 42-bar proportions and report boundaries around 0:56–1:04 support this broad division, not the exact instant of the pause.

transitions.title: A repeated note anchors the ascent
transitions.how: Near the close, a repeated D alternates with a rising chromatic line. The fixed note sustains dominant pressure while the upper notes climb, after which the figuration turns towards G major. The final full chord replaces the preceding alternation of registers with a single settled sonority. One player has supplied the changing upper line, the pedal-like repeated note and the cadence.
transitions.evidence: Score bars 37–38 alternate D with a chromatic ascent; bars 39–42 close in G major. The report’s strong 1:46 boundary and higher-level final span support the approximate map point. No exact chromatic note or bar is aligned.

facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players
Cantatas, Passions, the B minor Mass, organ and keyboard cycles, concertos, unaccompanied string music
composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.
composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
